Index Terms—Connect-4 robot, computer vision, HSV segmentation, trusted-state validation, closed-loop verification I. I NTRODUCTION Autonomous board-game robots are useful mechatronic benchmarks because they force perception, reasoning, and actuation to agree on the same physical state in real time [3]. A Connect-4 robot must read

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: the board, infer the next legal move, position a dispenser over the chosen column, and verify that the physical outcome matches the internal plan. The challenge is not only to solve each stage independently, but to prevent small perception or actuation errors from silently corrupting the game state. Prior work has treated the main subproblems separately. Vision papers show that canonical board rectification and per-cell inference are effective for structured tabletop games [4], [5]. HSV-based color segmentation remains attractive in robotic handling when illumination is reasonably controlled and the target

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: colors are well separated [6]. Chess-playing robots also show that robust physical manipulation of game pieces is often harder than the game reasoning itself [7]. Connect-4 simplifies the manipulator geometry because only lateral positioning is needed, but it still requires robust token-color recognition and gravity-aware validation. The gap addressed in this project is the lack of a tightly documented end-to-end Connect-4 implementation in which camera-based perception, trusted board-state acceptance, physical token placement, and post-move re-verification are all treated as one closed loop. For course deliverables, it is easy to report

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: a working classifier, a working minimax solver, or a working dispenser separately. The harder and more important question is whether the complete system keeps a trustworthy state when the real hardware misses, stalls, or sees ambiguous frames. This paper makes four concrete contributions. 1) It documents a complete vision-guided Connect-4 robot in which a trusted-state validator gates the board before action and a camera re-check gates the board after action. 2) It benchmarks three perception modes – HSV, Auto, and ML – and shows that HSV is the strongest practical operating mode under the tested indoor conditions. 3) It shows that the dominant real-world bottleneck is mechanical drop reliability, especially for long carriage

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: travel toward the edge columns, rather than image segmentation accuracy. 4) It reports representative end-to-end demonstrations with honest limits: the integrated robot closes the loop in the archived demos, while the separate 31/31 logic checks show that the state machine remained stable before hardware uncertainty entered the loop. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the most relevant literature and motivates the system boundary used here. Section III summarizes the integrated architecture and the final physical setup. Section IV explains the vision and state-estimation pipeline

Section VII discusses the main lessons and limitations. Section VIII concludes. II. R ELATED W ORK A. Board-State Extraction Wolflein and Arandjelovic decomposed chess-state extraction into board localization, homographic rectification, and square-level recognition [4]. That decomposition transfers well to Connect-4 because the board is still a fixed grid, but the classifier changes from piece identity to three states: empty, red, and yellow. Masouris and van Gemert later

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: showed that end-to-end learning can reduce hand-crafted geometry stages at the cost of a larger training burden [5]. For a course project with modest data, the modular route is more practical because each failure can be inspected directly. B. Color Segmentation Under Lighting Variation Akış and Dişlitaş showed that HSV-based object detection remains strong in robotic handling when color is the dominant cue and lighting is managed carefully [6]. Their findings match the Connect-4 setting: token hue is informative, while raw RGB intensity alone is less stable. The same literature

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: also warns that fixed thresholds weaken under large lighting shifts, which matters here because the board and tokens are glossy plastic surfaces. C. Game Robots and Embedded Decision Layers Board-game robots such as Gambit show that unconstrained manipulation of pieces, not game reasoning, is often the harder part of the problem [7]. On the decision side, depth-limited minimax with alpha-beta pruning remains a practical baseline for Connect-4 because the game is structured, discrete, and fully observable [8]. The missing piece is the interface between these subsystems: a robot still needs

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: a trusted physical board state before the search is meaningful, and a verified post-move state before the next turn is safe. III. passages.text: Mechanical Drop Reliability Dominates the Real Bottleneck Figure 4 reports the final token-drop success rates over 20 trials per column. Columns 1–3 achieved 100% success, columns 4 and 5 achieved 95%, column 6 achieved 90%, and column 7 dropped to 85%. The overall success rate was 95% across 140 drops. These numbers matter because they change the diagnosis of the system. The robot already sees the board well enough for play; what it does not yet do equally well is deliver the physical token to every column with the same

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: repeatability. The reason is the time-based carriage. Travel error accumulates as the commanded distance grows, so the edge columns are more exposed than the center columns. Once the carriage is correctly aligned, the encoder-coupled magazine release is much more repeatable than the carriage itself. That is why the

Integrated End-to-End Behavior The final materials reported an end-to-end cycle time from accepted board state to verified robot move ranging from 3 to 15 s, with a 7.5 s average. That number matters because it reflects what the user experiences, not just what the imageprocessing notebook can do in isolation. The reason for the gap between millisecond-scale perception and multi-second gameplay is that the full loop includes motion, settling time, and post-drop verification.

passages.text: Earlier benchmarking on the same project reported only 8.47 ms for rotation, 3.60 ms for perspective warp, and 0.76 ms for the deployed 5 × 5 Gaussian stage on the Pi, so the visible latency is dominated by mechanics and confirmation rather than by image processing itself. Figure 5 shows the system-level proof sequence used in the final demo story. A human move is first accepted into the trusted state, the robot then plans its response, and the next accepted frame confirms the post-drop board. This matters because it demonstrates

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: the actual closed loop, not just a sequence of isolated screenshots. The same final course materials also recorded 31/31 passed core checks spanning win detection, gravity-correct updates, validator rules, minimax edge cases, and simulator progressions. That result matters because it isolates the logic layer from the hardware layer. The reason it strengthens the overall project is that it shows the state machine and planner were stable before mechanical uncertainty entered the loop, even though it should not be read as a counted benchmark of full physical games. VII. D ISCUSSION

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: AND L IMITATIONS The strongest outcome of this project is not any one classifier score or any one demo video. It is the fact that the robot treats both perception and actuation as potentially fallible and therefore refuses to advance its internal state without evidence. The trusted-state validator protects the planner from impossible boards, and the post-drop re-check protects the planner from believing a move happened when the hardware actually missed. In a physical robot, that distinction is more valuable than a marginal gain in standalone classifier accuracy. The three-mode

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: comparison also leads to a practical, not ideological, conclusion. HSV is not universally better than learning-based methods, but it is the right default for the tested setup because its assumptions match the data that was actually collected: a fixed camera, a known blue frame, red and yellow tokens, and controlled indoor lighting. The ML and Auto modes remain useful because they show an extensible path beyond thresholding, but the current evidence does not justify displacing HSV as the primary runtime mode. The main limitation is the mechanical dispenser, especially the

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: time-based carriage. The inner columns prove that the concept works, but the outer-column degradation shows that the current actuation path is not yet uniformly reliable across the full board width. A carriage encoder or homing feedback would attack the dominant failure directly. This is the highestleverage hardware improvement because it addresses the part of the loop that the final data identifies as the actual bottleneck. The second major limitation is environmental robustness. The final tests were run with a fixed mounting geometry, a stable indoor setup, and the blue board

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: clearly separated from the background. That is a fair engineering boundary for a course robot, but it is not evidence of universal deployment robustness. Lighting shifts, glare, and domain changes remain real limits, especially for the fixed-threshold HSV path and the small-data ML path. The current system therefore demonstrates successful integrated operation under the tested conditions, not guaranteed generalization to arbitrary rooms or camera placements. VIII. C ONCLUSION This paper documented a complete vision-guided Connect-4 robot in which board reading, trusted-state acceptance, move planning, token placement, and camera-based re-verification form

passages.title: Paper
passages.text: one closed loop. The final results support four clear conclusions: the project achieved representative end-to-end integrated demonstrations, HSV was the strongest practical vision mode under the tested setup, mechanical drop reliability was the dominant real-world bottleneck, and the final system remained limited by lighting shift and open-loop carriage mechanics. The key lesson is therefore architectural as much as algorithmic. A modest mechatronics system becomes far more trustworthy when it treats camera inference and physical execution as hypotheses to be checked, not as facts to be assumed. That lesson generalizes beyond

passages.text: Connect-4 and is the main reason this project reaches a stronger final quality bar than a checklist-driven pipeline demo. ACKNOWLEDGMENT The authors thank Dr. Omar M. I NTRODUCTION Autonomous game-playing robots are compact testbeds for tightly coupled perception, cognition, and actuation [1]. The system reported here targets Connect-4: tokens fall under gravity once released above a column, so the actuator only needs repeatable lateral positioning at one horizontal axis. The required positional error is below half the column pitch (≈ 20 mm). This paper documents the final milestone state of the project. Earlier milestones validated the image processing pipeline in isolation and

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: characterized its per-operation cost on the embedded platform. The present milestone integrates that pipeline into a complete closed loop in which the camera is both the input sensor (for board reading) and the verification sensor (for post-move confirmation). Three subsystems are involved: • Perception and decision: a Raspberry Pi 4 running Python/OpenCV, a trusted-state validator, a depth-5 minimax solver, and a Flask-based operator dashboard. • Communication: a USB-serial channel at 9600 baud carrying a single ASCII column digit (’1’–’7’) and reverse-channel status tokens (READY, BUSY, MAG_PULSES, DONE). • Actuation: an

Either iterative deepening with a wall-clock budget or a learned policy prior would help

C ONCLUSION This paper has presented the final integrated state of the Vision-Based Connect-4 Robot. The system reads a Connect4 board with a Pi Camera, classifies the 42 cells via HSV, ML, or a hybrid Auto mode, validates the resulting board against six legality rules, plans a move with depth-5 alphabeta minimax, sends the chosen column to an Arduino over USB serial, and physically dispenses one token by

passages.title: MS4/5 final report
passages.text: sequencing a TT carriage motor and an encoder-coupled magazine motor through two L298N channels. After actuation, the camera is reused to verify the new state, closing the perception-decisionactuation loop. Measured per-cell classification accuracy is 98% (HSV), 96% (Auto), and 91% (ML); per-column drop success ranges from 100% (inner columns) to 85% (column 7); end-to-end task time averages between 3 and 15 seconds depending on column distance and minimax load; and all 31 game-logic unit tests pass on the Pi. The system meets the final milestone’s closed-loop and ML-bonus requirements, with

passages.text: youssef.salama@student.guc.edu.eg Abstract—This paper presents the design and implementation of an autonomous Vision-Based Connect-4 Robot, a mechatronic system that integrates computer vision, embedded computing, and robotic actuation. An RGB camera acquires frames of a standard 7×6 Connect-4 grid; a Python/OpenCV processing pipeline performs geometric normalization, intensity conditioning, noise suppression, and morphological filtering. An extracted gamestate matrix drives closed-loop motor commands evaluated via a Minimax algorithm, transmitted over a serial link to an Arduinocontrolled actuation stage. The full pipeline has been validated on a Raspberry Pi 4 (4 GB) and benchmarked against

passages.title: MS3 closed-loop integration
passages.text: a laptop platform. Execution times per operation range from 0.73 ms to 8.47 ms on the Raspberry Pi. Output image quality is bit-for-bit identical on both platforms. The mechanical assembly, modeled in SolidWorks, uses a magazine-and-slide dispensing mechanism with a servo-controlled gate for column selection. Index Terms—Connect-4, computer vision, image processing, Raspberry Pi, closed-loop motor control, OpenCV, SolidWorks, Arduino 1) Perception: a Pi Camera V2 capturing overhead RGB frames, followed by an OpenCV-based preprocessing pipeline; 2) Computation: a Raspberry Pi 4 (4 GB) running Python, extracting image features, computing game

This paper reports the system through Milestone 03: the image processing pipeline has been fully implemented, the hardware is completely fabricated and connected, and the realtime closed-loop integration has been established incorporating the camera as the primary sensing feedback element for intelligent actuation decisions. I. I NTRODUCTION II. R ELATED W ORK A. Board Detection and Game-State Extraction Extracting a

passages.text: complete game state from a camera image is the foundational perceptual task. Wölflein and Arandjelović [2] proposed a modular CNN pipeline for chess recognition—automated corner localization, homographic perspective rectification, and per-cell CNN inference—achieving greater than 98% per-square occupancy accuracy. This modular structure transfers directly to a 7×6 Connect-4 grid by replacing the six-class piece classifier with a three-class one (red token, yellow token, empty cell). Rezaei and Raihan [3] extended this line with a fully end-to-end model that eliminates the explicit rectification stage, reducing processing latency by removing the critical

passages.text: failure mode of missed corner detections. Autonomous game-playing robots are compelling mechatronic testbeds because they demand tightly integrated perception, cognition, and actuation operating in a real-time loop [1]. The robot described here targets Connect-4, a two-player, zerosum game in which the first player to align four same-colored discs—horizontally, vertically, or diagonally—wins. Tokens fall under gravity once released above the correct column, which simplifies the end-effector requirement: the arm must achieve repeatable lateral positioning over each column entry with an error smaller than half the column pitch (≈ 20 mm for a standard board), but need not execute a grasp-and-insert motion. T OKEN D ETECTION AND C OLOR S EGMENTATION Reliable identification of token color is the critical perceptual task that distinguishes Connect 4 perception from monochromatic chess-piece recognition. Ambient illumination in an uncontrolled laboratory environment can shift the apparent token hue by 20–40 degrees in RGB space, rendering fixed RGB thresholds unreliable. The Hue–Saturation–Value (HSV) color space is the de-facto standard for illuminationtolerant color segmentation because the hue channel is largely decoupled from intensity changes caused by shadow or lamp variation.
